ai_summary: Great Britain's wind output currently stands at 8.0 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output reaching 1.4 GW, which represents 13.9% of installed Scottish wind capacity. At the same time, Scottish carbon intensity sits at a clean 0 gCO2/kWh versus 144 gCO2/kWh GB-wide, highlighting Scotland's vast zero-carbon capability. Nevertheless, structural transmission bottlenecks across cross-border boundaries continue to prevent this renewable power from flowing freely to southern demand centres. As a direct consequence of these grid export limitations, Scottish generation curtailed so far today stands at 578 MWh at a constraint cost of about £38,660. To replace this lost clean power, thermal generation had to be dispatched downstream, resulting in an estimated 109,820 m3 of gas burned elsewhere and producing an avoidable 202 tonnes of CO2. Extrapolating today’s figures yields an estimated total yearly cost of curtailment of £14 million. When socialised through national balancing service charges across total demand, this increases everybody's invoice in the UK by an estimated £0.05/MWh. Expediting transmission network infrastructure upgrades remains essential to capture stranded green electricity, eliminate compensatory fossil reliance, and protect consumer energy bills.
